intro:33: Al-Ahzab is a Madinan surah. One of the themes that brings its subjects together is the Prophet’s ﷺ steadfastness amid many kinds of harm and pressure. There was a military coalition of Quraysh and allied tribes, with some Jews taking part in stirring up the confederates; there were also hypocrites within the community, watching for opportunities and spreading doubts. The surah is not confined to the battlefield. It also addresses matters within the Prophet’s household and the way people treated him ﷺ. His wives, may Allah be pleased with them, had asked for more generous living expenses, and were given a choice between the worldly life and its adornment, and Allah, His Messenger and the Hereafter: «But if you seek Allah and His Messenger and the Final Abode, then Allah has prepared for those who do good among you a great reward» [Al-Ahzab 33:29].

This was one of the responsibilities of married life; it is not to be equated with the hostility of combatants or the plotting of hypocrites. Rather, it shows the many responsibilities the Prophet ﷺ carried while remaining steadfast in obeying his Lord. Another example was that some guests lingered in his home, enjoying conversation, while he felt too shy to ask them to leave. Revelation clarified the matter: «without lingering for conversation. Such [behavior] causes annoyance to the Prophet; he is too shy to express it to you, but Allah is not shy of [telling] the truth» [Al-Ahzab 33:53]. In the same surah that describes this hurt comes the declaration of his honour among the highest company: «Indeed, Allah sends His blessings upon the Prophet, and His angels pray for him» [Al-Ahzab 33:56]. The number of people who hurt a believer on earth does not, then, establish that the believer is insignificant before Allah. Patience and contentment during hardship may be a means of attaining a higher standing with Him.

The way these matters are addressed shows how clear explanations close off opportunities for malicious allegations. The attribution of an adopted son to someone other than his father is explicitly invalidated at the beginning of the surah. Allah also explains that the Prophet’s ﷺ marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with her, took place by His command: «When Zayd no longer had desire for her, We gave her to you in marriage» [Al-Ahzab 33:37]. Revelation likewise explained the etiquette of entering his home and departing from it. Money and relationships with women can have a profound effect on the reputation of someone who calls others to Allah. Good intentions alone are not enough; that person needs upright, transparent dealings that do not expose the message to suspicion.

Surat At-Tawbah describes people who criticise the distribution of charity according to the share they receive: «if they are given something thereof, they are pleased, but if they are not given, they are enraged» [At-Tawbah 9:58]. Its recipients are then specified, beginning with «Alms [i.e., zakah] is only for the poor and the needy» and concluding with «as ordained by Allah» [At-Tawbah 9:60]. Its distribution is therefore not governed by the critics’ wishes, nor is it a personal whim of the Messenger ﷺ. The Mothers of the Believers were reminded of their responsibility towards what was recited in their homes: «And remember what is recited in your homes of Allah’s verses and [prophetic] wisdom[28]» [Al-Ahzab 33:34]. Closeness to the Prophet’s household calls for greater care in obeying Allah, and someone looking for an opportunity may use those around a caller to Allah as a means of attacking that person. A particularly clear example is the slander against Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, when people spoke accusations from which Allah declared her innocent. The harm was directed at the Prophet’s ﷺ household and honour [Al-Bukhari 4141].

An attack may begin by trying to undermine confidence in revelation. When the objection proves unsound, its proponent may turn against the person conveying the message, then against that person’s family and associates. Allah says: «It is We Who have sent down the Reminder[5], and it is We Who will preserve it[6]» [Al-Hijr 15:9]. What an objector supposes to be a defect may become the occasion for revealing an aspect of the truth that people had not noticed. One illustration compares the truth to a body of light: whenever someone tries to wound it, light emerges. Answering an objection may thus make the truth clearer. Moving from discussing a statement to trying to discredit its speaker by every possible means, however, may deprive people of good from which they could benefit.

When a person’s good qualities predominate and their benefit is extensive, one lapse should not be made to erase all their merits. A comparison that helps illustrate the effect of abundant good is the Prophet’s ﷺ statement about water: «If the water is two pitchers, it will bear no impurity» [Abu Dawud 63]. The Arabic measure is qullatayn [قلتين], two large water vessels. This hadith concerns ritual purification; it is mentioned here as an analogy, not to turn a person’s error into something right. The point is that a limited error should not overshadow extensive good, and that a person’s worth should be recognised alongside their shortcomings. People do not merely need words about religion detached from action; they need examples in whose conduct they can see its effects.

This is why Surat Al-Furqan concludes by describing «The slaves of the Most Compassionate are those who walk on earth humbly[36]» [Al-Furqan 25:63]. They are human beings living among people, just as the Messenger ﷺ lived among them, although his opponents said: «What kind of messenger is this who eats food and walks in the markets?[2]» [Al-Furqan 25:7]. People may see honesty, trustworthiness and mercy in a fellow student, an employer or a family member, and understand through this example what description alone had not made clear. When the role model’s mistake is exaggerated, the consequences may extend beyond criticism of that mistake, because some people fail to distinguish the religion from the shortcomings of those who profess it.

A flawed way of judging others is to let present emotion cancel a history of kindness. This is illustrated by the warning against ingratitude towards a husband: «If you have always been good (benevolent) to one of them». The hadith explains that when she then sees something she dislikes, she says: «I have never received any good from you» [Al-Bukhari 29]. In this picture, long-standing kindness is forgotten because of something disliked on one occasion. A reflective reader needs to beware of applying such a standard when judging people. The danger of losing those who carry knowledge is explained by the Prophet’s ﷺ words: «Verily, Allah does not take away knowledge by snatching it from the people; rather, He takes away knowledge with the death of the scholars» [Al-Bukhari 100]. Knowledge clarifies the truth and shows people how to act on it. Preserving its words alone cannot replace the people who understand and convey it.

The first way a caller to Allah protects both themselves and their message is by remaining upright, not by appeasing opponents through contradicting what they call others to. The surah therefore opens with: «O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites» [Al-Ahzab 33:1]. Mindfulness of Allah and obedience are fundamental when facing harm. It is from this starting point that we read the scene of the believers surrounded by the confederates.
33:9: The Quran asks the believers to reconsider an event they themselves experienced, but from a perspective taught by Allah: «remember Allah’s favor upon you». Recounting the campaign to those who witnessed it is not merely repeating familiar news. People may share a journey, then disagree on returning about which actions were right and who acted well or badly. Simply witnessing an event does not ensure a sound judgement of it. Revelation presents the event by Allah’s standard, correcting assessments of actions and revealing movements of the heart that people cannot see. Describing Uhud, Allah says: «When two parties[57] from among you were about to lose courage, but Allah was their protector» [Al Imran 3:122]. An inclination towards losing courage occurs within the heart; others may not see it, and the person may not appreciate its consequences, but it is not hidden from Allah.

The Quran thus teaches its reader not to confine the reality of an event to what the eye has seen. This is also why Allah recounted to Musa, peace be upon him, his own past when entrusting him with the message: «And We had already conferred favor upon you before» «when We inspired your mother, saying» [Ta-Ha 20:37–38], followed by «‘Put him into the casket, then cast it into the river. The river will carry it to the shore, and he will be picked up by one who is an enemy to Me and enemy to him.’ I bestowed upon you love from Myself[9]» [Ta-Ha 20:39]. Someone who looked only at outward causes would see a mother afraid for her baby, a chest carried on the water, a household it reached and a woman who loved him. Revelation, however, reveals Allah’s direction throughout these stages: He inspired the mother, guided the chest and bestowed love.

The story should therefore not be told as a series of disconnected coincidences with no One directing them. The same applies to the confederates: visible forces arrived, then Allah sent against them a wind and forces the believers could not see. Behind the visible causes is the One who brings them about and determines them, glorified is He. Beneficial remembrance includes looking back at moments of rescue in one’s own life to recognise overlooked blessings. A person may survive a journey in which an accident nearly killed them, yet remember only the terror and forget how Allah protected them. A friend may offer comfort by reminding them of such moments, rather than adding to the list of their sufferings. Satan may bring back the past in a form that shows a person nothing but fear and pain, drawing them into regret and objection to divine decree. Faith retells the story with an awareness of Allah’s protection and direction within the causes.

For this reason, when something unwelcome happens, the Prophet ﷺ forbade dwelling on “if only”, saying: «Indeed, 'if' opens the way before the devil to act» [Muslim 2664]. The point is not to keep replaying what did not happen, but to benefit from what did happen and recognise the Lord’s favour within it. Just as Iblis refused to submit to Allah’s command, he wants to lead people to object to His decree. Explaining «indeed, man is very ungrateful to his Lord[5]» [Al-Adiyat 100:6], Al-Hasan said that such a person counts misfortunes and forgets the Lord’s blessings [Ibn Kathir’s commentary on Al-Adiyat 100:6]. Someone may live for twenty years, enjoying health, provision and well-being for nineteen and a half, then undergo six months of hardship and speak of their entire life as though nothing remained but those months. This illustrates how dwelling on pain can conceal the blessings that preceded and accompanied it.

The verse begins with the campaign’s outcome before describing its scenes: a blessing from Allah when the forces came, their repulsion by a wind and unseen forces, and Allah’s full awareness of the believers’ actions. The contrast between «[enemy] forces came against you[7]» and «We sent against them a violent wind and forces that you could not see[8]» shows that Allah’s support is not confined to the form of strength a servant expects. The response was not simply troops against troops; means of victory came together beyond what they could observe. The campaign of the confederates was less a matter of extensive combat than a battle within hearts. The Prophet ﷺ and his Companions dug the trench and continued resisting the danger of siege, amid a broken treaty, the hypocrites’ discouragement and some skirmishes. Then Allah turned their enemy away.

The summary therefore concludes with «And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do». A trial may not be intended to secure a particular worldly gain for the believer, but to reveal what the believer will do when besieged and whether they will emerge with firmer faith. The trial of Tabuk is comparable: one of its greatest tests was choosing to set out with the Messenger ﷺ in the heat, at a time when the fruit was ripe, then enduring the journey’s hardship, even though the expedition did not end in a decisive battle with the Romans. The words «who followed him in the hour of hardship [at Tabūk]» [At-Tawbah 9:117] highlight the value of following in hardship. The decisive moment of choosing may itself be the steep obstacle that must be surmounted, bringing to mind «Yet he did not make his way through the steep path[3]» [Al-Balad 90:11], without reducing every demand of the journey to that one moment.

At Uhud, pain taught the believers what simply hearing the command had not been enough to establish within them. They learnt the consequences of obeying the Messenger ﷺ, and after what had befallen them they were addressed: «Do not lose heart nor grieve, for you have the upper hand, if you are [truly] believers» [Al Imran 3:139]. The standard of superiority here is tied to living out faith, not merely to the military result. A servant may lose something worldly and, through patience and contentment, gain a closeness to Allah that cannot be matched by the wealth they regret losing. Someone whose aim is the Hereafter assesses loss and gain differently from someone who sees only what is immediately received in this world.

Learning is not entirely theoretical. A child may be warned about a hot cup without paying attention, then touch it, experience its heat and become cautious afterwards even about a cup whose temperature they do not know. This illustrates the effect of experience; it does not mean that a believer should wait for harm before accepting a truthful account. In Qarun’s story, some people were dazzled by his splendour and said: «Oh, would that we had the like of what Korah has been given! He is indeed a man of great fortune» [Al-Qasas 28:79]. Those who had been given knowledge, however, said before the earth swallowed him: «Woe to you! Allah’s reward is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds» [Al-Qasas 28:80]. When Allah caused the earth to swallow him and his home, those captivated by him discovered what the people of knowledge had already understood.

A person who knows the truth may die before witnessing the collapse of falsehood, without this undermining their certainty. Belief does not require that a person see the outcome within their lifetime. This distinguishes faith in the unseen, with which Allah describes the mindful—«those who believe in the unseen» [Al-Baqarah 2:3]—from making faith dependent on sight, as in the Israelites’ words: «we will never believe you until we see Allah openly» [Al-Baqarah 2:55]. An example of this certainty is Abu Bakr’s response, may Allah be pleased with him, on hearing the account of the Prophet’s ﷺ Night Journey. He affirmed that if the Prophet had said this, then he had certainly spoken the truth [Al-Hakim, Al-Mustadrak 4461]. What matters is that the report be established as coming from the truthful one, not that the listener must first have seen everything he describes.

A trial’s purpose may be fulfilled before the feared event takes place. When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was tested with sacrificing his son, submission and the precedence of love for Allah became apparent; then came the ransom: «This was indeed a revealing test» «And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice[24]» [As-Saffat 37:106–107]. The purpose was not simply the loss of his son, but the obedience the test revealed. Musa likewise told his people: «The earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whom He wills of His slaves, but the outcome is for those who fear Allah» [Al-Araf 7:128]. That truth is not altered by how long or short Pharaoh’s rule lasts. But they said: «We were oppressed before you came to us and after you came», as though asking what had changed in their circumstances after believing. His answer was: «It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land to see how you will do» [Al-Araf 7:129].

He shifted their attention from Pharaoh’s removal alone to their responsibility afterwards. Being given authority is itself a test, and someone who survived hardship may weaken when prosperity opens up. The question of conduct remains in both situations: «We test you with bad and good as a trial» [Al-Anbiya 21:35]. Allah can remove the causes of harm surrounding believers, but He tests them so that their actions within those circumstances become apparent. He says: «if Allah had willed, He could have subjected them to punishment, but [He ordered you to fight] to test some of you by means of others» [Muhammad 47:4]. One application is that disagreements among people working for Allah’s religion are not merely a problem one wishes would disappear altogether; they test a person’s character and intention. Are they seeking the truth or defending their own desires?

Will they treat their brother fairly, or attack him in order to tear him down? They are likewise tested by desire, by unlawful money offered to them, by maintaining prayer amid the demands of work, and by the patience required in family life and travel. Allah says: «indeed, among your wives and your children are some who are enemies[2] to you, so beware of them» [At-Taghabun 64:14]. Even cherished relationships may become a test if they draw a servant away from obedience to the Lord. Worldly life is a realm of changing circumstances, unlike the bliss of the people of Paradise, of whom the Prophet ﷺ said: «they would glorify and praise Allah as easily as you breathe» [Muslim 2835].

A servant should not wait for a life free of every obstacle before beginning to worship and obey Allah: obedience amid these changes is part of the test itself. It is a mistake to make sincerity conditional on circumstances changing, saying that one will give if provision increases, then becoming miserly when it does. The Quran describes this: «There are some among them who made a covenant with Allah: “If He gives us out of His bounty, we will surely spend in charity and be among the righteous.”», followed by «But when He did give them out of His bounty, they grew stingy and turned away in aversion» [At-Tawbah 9:75–76]. Worship and obedience do not mean performing exactly the same deeds to the same extent in every situation. Someone who is ill may be unable to do what they did in health, but can worship through patience and contentment. The Prophet ﷺ said: «If a person falls ill or travels, he shall be credited with whatever good deeds he used to perform while being at home and in good health» [Al-Bukhari 2996].

What is required is to follow what Allah wants of the servant within their ability in each situation, rather than making one particular set of circumstances a condition for obedience. In this way, «And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do» remains present in ease and hardship, while waiting for relief as well as when relief becomes visible.
33:10: The verse describes not an ordinary encounter with an enemy, but overwhelming encirclement and pressure: «from above you and from below you[9]». There is a difference between fearing that a group may lose a battle and feeling that it is surrounded in its own homeland, with its very survival threatened. Merely facing swords is a severe test. When asked why the martyr is spared the trial of the grave, the Prophet ﷺ said: «The flashing of the swords above his head is trial enough» [An-Nasai 2053]. An example of sincere faith in such a situation is the man who believed, then fought at Uhud until he was wounded and died. He entered Paradise before having offered a single prayer to Allah [Abu Dawud 2537]. The value of a stand is not measured only by the time it takes.

At the battle of the confederates, the danger of confrontation was compounded by the sense of encirclement and threats from several directions. One reason the test was so severe was that it came after Uhud, when memories of defeat were still present. The possibility of collapse therefore felt particularly real. At Badr, the believers had faced something unfamiliar, and the Quran describes some of their fear: «as if they were being driven towards death while they were looking on» [Al-Anfal 8:6]. The victory at Badr was then present in the minds of those keen to march out at Uhud, as though the previous result would be repeated. When the confederates came, it was instead the memories of losing Hamzah and Musab, may Allah be pleased with them, and of what had happened to the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud that were present.

A person may assess an approaching situation by their most recent painful experience, imagining defeat before it occurs and allowing its possibilities to grow within them. The test of the confederates was not merely the possibility of death. It tested trust in Allah when frightening circumstances converged and those spreading discouragement began attacking the promise itself. The Quran presents the terror of this siege through its effect on those who witnessed it. Describing an event’s impact on a person may convey its severity more effectively than listing its external details. A scene in an examination hall illustrates this: a female student undergoing severe personal difficulties received the question paper and fainted. The student beside her saw what happened before reading their own paper, and what they saw in another person intensified their apprehension about the unknown.

The example does not explain what the questions contained; it shows how fear can be understood from the condition of someone who has faced the situation. A similar shift towards the effects of terror appears in the description of the Hour’s convulsion: «On the Day when you see it, every nursing mother will abandon her baby, and every pregnant woman will miscarry. You will see people as though they are drunk, while they are not drunk, but the punishment of Allah is severe» [Al-Hajj 22:2]. What must the terror be like to make a nursing mother forget the infant in her arms? Here, the effects of the siege unfold through eyes, hearts and thoughts. The words «your eyes grew wild [in horror]» depict eyes unable to remain still from sheer alarm, turning as though asking: where will danger come from?

And where is the way out? The eye settles when a person is reassured and becomes restless when afraid. This reveals a connection with the Prophet’s ﷺ words: «my comfort has been provided in prayer» [An-Nasai 3939]. The Arabic expression qurratu ʿaynī [قُرَّةُ عَيْنِي] means the delight or comfort of my eyes. Instead of eyes looking in every direction and a heart pulled between fears, the worshipper’s gaze settles on the place of prostration and the heart turns to Allah. Prayer gathers the heart around its Lord after fear has scattered its attention. Hudhayfah also reported: «When anything distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he prayed» [Abu Dawud 1319], meaning when something distressing befell him. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, testified that on the night before Badr the Prophet ﷺ prayed and supplicated until morning [Ahmad 1161].

A practical lesson from this scene is that someone facing illness, a problem or financial distress should turn to prayer and avoid rushing into a major decision at the height of agitation. They can pray, supplicate and become calmer, then consider the matter with renewed awareness of their need for Allah and the true nature of what people compete over. This accords with placing prayer and supplication before proceeding with a matter in istikharah, as the Prophet ﷺ taught his Companions [Al-Bukhari 6382]. Prayer is not merely a break from thinking; it is a return to Allah, to judge things soundly and seek His guidance to what is right.

Then comes «the hearts reached the throats», an expression for fear reaching its utmost, as though the heart had risen into the throat from distress. The effect is no longer visible only in the eyes’ movement; it has reached deep within the person. The verse then moves from the body’s outward condition to what passes through the mind: «you began to entertain various thoughts about Allah[10]». The danger is that pressure may turn into doubt about the path and Allah’s promise. In Arabic, zāghat [زاغت, grew unsettled] and balaghat [بلغت, reached] are in the past tense, while taẓunnūna [تظنون, you think] is in the present. One reflection on this shift is the continuing renewal of thoughts: physical fear may lessen, or a person may find a safe place, while the mind goes on circling through possibilities without rest.

The lengthened sound of the Arabic word aẓ-ẓunūnā [الظنونا, thoughts or suppositions] also suits the picture of these successive thoughts. Satan may raise questions about the religion’s future or the value of migration and sacrifice, seeking to move a person from fear for themselves to doubt about the very basis of their faith. This does not mean that these thoughts were identical in every heart. One interpretation is that the plural includes both good expectations among the steadfast and bad expectations among others. Another is that it refers to different kinds of bad expectation according to degrees of weakness: some doubt the truth of the message, while others do not deny the Messenger but lose hope that the truth will prevail and relief will come.

There is a difference between fear accompanied by a struggle against one’s own weakness and accepting attacks on Allah and His Messenger; the situation’s severity does not erase it. Hardship may reveal what ease does not. Someone may see gentleness in a friend during quiet days, then be surprised by insults and harshness when a dispute arises. As pressure increases, more of what was hidden within becomes apparent. The perfection of the Prophet’s ﷺ steadfastness appears when different pressures converge without turning him from obedience to his Lord. One connection with the surah’s opening is: «Allah has not made for any man two hearts inside him» [Al-Ahzab 33:4]. Just as two hearts do not occupy one chest, the believer needs a united direction, rather than being scattered by conflicting desires, so that turning towards the Hereafter is not merely talk that disappears at the first threat to worldly interests.

In the account of Rabiah ibn Kab, may Allah be pleased with him, after he had served the Prophet ﷺ, the Prophet told him: «Ask (anything you like)». He replied: «I ask your company in Paradise». When the Prophet ﷺ asked: «Or anything else besides it», he answered: «That is all (what I require)» [Muslim 489]. His goal was clear, so he did not turn from it to another request. This clarity of direction helps us understand what is required of a heart besieged by fears: not to forget its goal with Allah.
33:11: «There» marks the moment of the real test: encirclement, unsettled eyes, hearts rising to throats and renewed thoughts converge, and «the believers were tested and were severely shaken». Being described as believers does not mean being spared the terror of trial. Believers’ hearts may be tested with this degree of severity. The shaking resembles what happens to trees: weak leaves fall, what has no root cannot withstand the movement, while what is deeply rooted in the soil remains firm. So it is with faith. A slight doubt may shake a heart that has not been nourished by the Quran or grounded in certainty, while another heart withstands hardships the first could not bear.

It is not enough to wait for every doubt to seek its answer while neglecting the foundation of one’s relationship with Allah. The root of faith should be strengthened before the shaking begins, rather than waiting for a crisis to start building it. A believer may emerge from a trial having practised forms of worship and obedience that would not have appeared in ease. A student accustomed to long hours of sleep may find, as an important exam approaches, a diligence and endurance they never displayed in their free time. Urgent need may reveal an ability previously unused. Similarly, someone who thinks fasting and night prayer too difficult may spend part of Ramadan in devotional retreat with supportive companions, and discover that they can fast and pray more than they expected.

Circumstances, motivation and companionship together may bring out previously latent deeds. A trial may draw forth patience, awareness of need and trust in Allah that raise a person’s standing with Him. The hadith states that those most severely tested are the prophets, then those most like them in excellence, followed by the next most like them. The Prophet ﷺ then said: «A man is tried according to his religion» [At-Tirmidhi 2398]. The severity of a trial alone does not therefore show that Allah has abandoned a believer; it may open the way to a standing that an easy life alone would not bring. Another wisdom of testing is to mature and strengthen the soul over time. Just as food needs what will cook it through, the fruit of experience does not appear in the soul merely by wishing for maturity.

Training a muscle by lifting weights against resistance and gradually increasing its capacity helps illustrate this meaning. Allah may likewise nurture a servant through a trial they endure steadfastly, then enable them to face what follows with experience and firmness they did not previously possess. Those who benefit here are those who remain patient and upright; not everyone who undergoes hardship emerges in the same condition. A young person may not recognise some people’s traits until entering work and trade, suffering deception or loss, and learning to check matters carefully and judge whom to trust. Long experience can improve advice. During the Ascension, when fifty prayers were prescribed, Musa advised the Prophet ﷺ to ask his Lord for a reduction, referring to his experience with the Israelites. Repeated returns followed until the prayers became five [Muslim 162].

His understanding of what people struggle with was the fruit of long experience, and those who came after him benefited from it. This is another aspect beyond obedience appearing in one particular situation: experience develops an insight through which a person understands what they face. The shaking also exposes the hypocrite and the weak, distinguishing the truthful from the hesitant. Allah says: «Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in, until He distinguishes the evil from the good[86]» [Al Imran 3:179]. Intensifying trials upon believers should therefore not be read as proof that their path is false. In the accounts of the messengers we read: «Until when the messengers lost all hope and realized that they were dismissed as liars, Our help came to them» [Yusuf 12:110], and concerning rain: «It is He Who sends down rain after they have lost hope, and spreads His mercy» [Ash-Shura 42:28].

When available means diminish, Allah’s power does not diminish. Hope remains attached to Him, not to a calculation of the visible means left to a servant. Yaqub’s grief for Yusuf, peace be upon them both, lasted until the Quran described him: «And his eyes turned white[33] because of suppressing his grief» [Yusuf 12:84]. Near the story’s conclusion came his words: «I certainly sense the fragrance of Joseph» [Yusuf 12:94]. Throughout that long period, his patience, hope and need for Allah became apparent. Had the separation ended after a few days, the successive moments in the story’s later stages would not have appeared in the same way. Recalling this does not set a time for relief in every hardship; it guards against despair of Allah’s mercy when the wait is long.

After the confederates departed, the Prophet ﷺ said: «From now onwards we will go to attack them (i.e. the infidels) and they will not come to attack us» [Al-Bukhari 4110]. The report repeats that the Muslims themselves would march out to them. In that event, severe hardship preceded a visible change in the Muslims’ circumstances; it was not the end of their path. One way of drawing lessons is to recall stages of the Prophet’s life amid the changing circumstances of the Muslim community: weakness, then a victory such as Badr, wounds such as Uhud, a formidable coalition, then conquest. A group or individual may experience some of these conditions, and their lifetime may fall within one stage rather than encompass the whole story. They should not judge the journey’s ending solely by the scene they themselves inhabit.

One such comparison likens the Islamic caliphate’s period of strength to Badr, its subsequent setbacks to Uhud, and the gathering of opponents to the confederates. This is an analogy for reflection, not a prophetic report assigning every stage of history. Believers may gain strength and authority in some lands without this being universal. Hope for relief is therefore not confined to waiting for the Mahdi’s appearance. The purpose of the reflection remains to preserve one’s worship and obedience within one’s own place in the trial, strengthen one’s bond with Allah, and avoid treating delayed hopes as the failure of the Lord’s promise.
33:12: When the shaking intensified, what had been concealed in ease emerged. A hypocrite who uses the language of faith in ordinary circumstances may lose self-control under trial, allowing objection to pass their lips. The first thing revealed here was an attack on the promise itself: «Allah and His Messenger did not promise us but delusion!». Pressure had moved them from fear for themselves to bad assumptions about Allah and His Messenger, to the point that they described the promise as deception. These are among the most dangerous words of discouragement. They go beyond complaining about the difficulty of the path and try to persuade those following it that their original choice was mistaken and that the good news they received has no reality.

A person may become slow to obey, then go beyond weakening themselves to discourage others. Not everyone who falls into some of this is equivalent to a complete hypocrite. A Muslim may have both a branch of faith and a trait of hypocrisy; the danger is allowing that trait to continue until it corrupts the heart. After listing traits of hypocrisy, the hadith states: «whoever has one of the following four characteristics will have one characteristic of hypocrisy unless and until he gives it up» [Al-Bukhari 34]. These traits include lying, betrayal of trust, treachery and abusive wrongdoing in disputes. The more habitual they become, the greater their danger, while the distinction remains between falling into a blameworthy trait and losing the foundation of faith altogether.

The mere appearance of a description in a passage condemning disbelievers or hypocrites is not enough to judge that every Muslim who resembles them in some actions has left the religion. Descriptions and deeds are not all of the same degree. One interpretation is that «those with sickness in their hearts» here includes those with weak faith, not only complete hypocrites. People’s assumptions differ according to the weakness within their hearts, and sharing a time of fear does not erase those differences. A believer therefore reads the description out of concern that discouragement and bad assumptions may begin to take root within themselves, not to declare themselves blameless and confine the verse’s danger to others.

The Arabic verb yaqūlu [يقول, says] is in the present tense. It brings before us this repeated speech, intended to circulate, rather than a single statement now over. As pressure intensifies, the tongue exposes what had been hidden, and a message of despair may pass from one troubled soul to a group whose steadfastness it weakens. Trial thus reveals that the most dangerous loss is not comfort, but beginning to interpret Allah’s promise as a deception instead of turning to Him in need and remaining steadfast in obedience.
